paragraphs: Qayma lan: kol ebar sheim niqqab – terepa, vehu haddin im nittal o chaser. velaken heeleti bitshuba besipri haqqadosh "rab-pealim" - beishsha sheppatecha hattarnegolet velo matzea haqqurqeban, veomeret shebbari lah shello nimtza bah qurqeban, veen lah litlot bechatul, hare zo terepa bevadday, veen lomar: ek tihyeh metziut kazo shettihyeh chasera haqqurqeban mittechilla! ella matrepinan lah. vesham hebeti dibre haggaon "chakam tzebi" za"l besiman y', ammud d', shehittir bammaaseh shehaya, shehiyyatah chasrat leb; beamero shei epshar lihyot belo leb, velaken nitla shehaya, veneebad kesheppitchah hattarnegolet, "y chatul vekayyotze, vezo sheppatecha lo hirgisha. vechalequ alayv kamma gedolim, vedachu horaato zot bishte yadayim; upasequ apillu beleb dei epshar lichyot shaa achat biladayv kepi hatteba – en tolin beneebad lehattir, ella kol heka dela chazu bah leb – terepa, veen litmoahh al hammetziut shehi neged hatteba.

clarification.explanation: The halachic rule: any organ whose perforation would render an animal or bird "treifah" (unfit for eating) — the same applies if that organ was entirely removed or missing from the start. Therefore Rabbi Yosef Chaim rules: a woman who opened a chicken and did not find a gizzard (a digestive organ) in it, and states clearly that no gizzard was found, and it cannot be attributed to a cat having removed it — the chicken is certainly treifah, and one may not say "it is impossible for it to have lived this way from birth without a gizzard" and permit it on that doubt. Rabbi Yosef Chaim brings a dissenting opinion (Chacham Tzvi) that in a case of a missing heart, one may attribute it to the heart having been lost after slaughter by a cat, but many Sages rejected this view and established that even for an organ without which life is impossible (like the heart) — if it is not found, the animal is treifah, and one may not attribute this to it having been "lost" against the animal's nature.
takeaways: If a vital organ that should exist is not found at all upon inspection, the animal/bird is certainly treifah — one should not speculate that the organ was "lost" after death.

paragraphs: Hakkabed shel op nechelaq lishne chalaqim, echad gadol veechad qatan; vecheleq haqqatan, apillu nittal kullo, kasher, kol zeman shecheleq haggadol qayyam vehu bari veshalem. amenam cheleq haggadol - im nittal o nirqab meqom hammara, maqom shehi teluya bo – terepa; veayyen baacharonim, siman m'. vehinneh hakkabed yesh bo inyanim harbeh shemmetarepim, vehu: ki lipamim yimmatze hakkabed yabesh shenniprak batztzipporen, veyesh bazeh kamma chilluqe dinim beshiur hayyobesh ubemah neda shiur zeh; veken gam ken yesh chilluqim bimqomot hayyobesh; gam od yimmatze lipamim shennimmoq hakkabed, dehaynu, sheddam yotze mibbesar hakkabed shennimmoq vehaya laddam; vegam yimmatze sheyyihyeh hakkabed qasheh keeben; ubekol ellu hammiqrim yesh chilluqe dinim ketubim beshulchan aruk ubapposeqim. al-ken bene-habbayit kaasher yiru dabar middebarim ellu, yebiuhu lehammoreh lishol et piv; vaapillu bishar shinnuyim sheen metarepim, kegon shehakkabed napucha o hitlia, yishalu lehammoreh. veken name od, im matzeu machat bakkabed - ben gedola, ben qetanna – terepa. vetzarik gam ken sheyyabiu lehammoreh veyireh, veaz hu yeesor et haasur veyattir et hammuttar.

clarification.explanation: A fowl's liver is made of two parts — large and small. If the small part is entirely removed, the fowl is still kosher, as long as the large part is whole and healthy. But in the large part, if it was removed or decayed at the point where the bile duct is attached — it is treifah. There are many conditions in the liver requiring examination: a dry liver that crumbles under a fingernail (with distinctions based on the degree and location of the dryness), a "melted" liver (where blood emerges from the tissue instead of actual flesh), a liver hard as stone, and so on. All of these require clarification from a halachic authority. Changes that do not render it treifah (swelling, worms) should also be brought for examination. And if a needle is found in the liver, whether large or small, the animal is treifah — this too requires the authority's examination, to forbid what is forbidden and permit what is permitted.
takeaways: Any unusual change in the liver (dryness, melting, hardness, a needle) must be examined by a halachic authority in every case, even if it is uncertain whether it renders the animal treifah.

paragraphs: Im patechu hattarnegolet o shear op verau shechasera hammara, az qorea hakkabed sheti vaereb vetoem bilshono, veim taam mar – keshera. veha debaenan liqroa hakkabed, haynu lekattechilla, abal bediabad im lo qareu hakkabed, ella raq taamu hakkabed mibbachutz umatzeu bo taam mar – keshera; veim qerauhu sheti vaereb velo taamu merirut, az yiqra kol hassimponot, sheqqorin bearbe "aruq" (oreqim), veim matza betokam taam mar, keshera; veayyen "binat-adam", shaar issur vehetter, siman sh"z besopo; veken im taamu et bene-meayim sheqqorin bearbe "mitztzarin" (meayim daqqim), umatzeu taam mar, keshera; veken hu haddin im tamo haqqurqeban sheqqorin bearbi "gantzi" vehaya mar kelaana, keshera; veken hor haddin im tamo hattechol vehaya mar, dikshera; abal im taamu bachalal haggup umatzeu bo taam mar, la mehanne lehakshir; dela ameru ella bimqomot hassemukim lemara, kegon qurqeban utechol ubene-meayim, demilleta dishkicha hi shettishshapek hammara alehem, abal lo bishar meqomot; veayyen "shebet-yeuddeh". ukeshehattarnegolet shemena o hammara shellah qetanna umekusseh beshumman, velipamim tihyeh qetanna ketippat zebub, vegaven shellah yaroq "atztzepar" (yaroq tzahob) sheddomeh letzoat haop, velipamim yaroq kekarti, tzarik beqiut limtzo otah mechamat qetanna, vehi mekussa beshumman o mekusseh betok oreq echad dehaynu simpon shebbakkabed, velipamim nimtza besop habbene-meayim; al-ken bene-habbayit, im lo matzeu hammara, yabiu hattarnegolet lipne hammoreh, veyibdoq vichappes veyimtza.

clarification.explanation: If a chicken or other fowl was opened and no gallbladder (bile sac) was found — the solution: the liver is torn lengthwise and widthwise and tasted with the tongue; if there is a bitter taste, the fowl is kosher (since the bile poured its taste onto the liver). This is required as the primary practice, but after the fact, if only the outside of the liver was tasted and a bitter taste was found — it is kosher. If it was torn entirely and no bitterness was found, the bronchial tubes (arteries) are torn open, and if bitterness is found there — it is kosher. The same applies if a bitter taste is found in the small intestines, the gizzard, or the spleen — it is kosher. But if a bitter taste is found in another part of the body cavity, this does not help to permit it, since the leniency applies only to places adjacent to the bile that plausibly received its spillage. One must be careful: sometimes the bile is very small (like a fly's droplet), greenish-yellow or green in color, covered in fat, or located at the end of the intestines — therefore if it is not found, the chicken should be brought to a halachic authority for careful examination.
takeaways: A visibly missing gallbladder can be resolved by finding a bitter taste in the liver, the bronchial tubes, the small intestines, the gizzard, or the spleen — but not elsewhere in the body.
The bile can be very small and hidden — an expert authority should examine carefully before declaring it absent.

paragraphs: Hannashim neemanot bitimat hakkabed; velaken im bene-habbayit rau shello nimtzet hammara, veishah achat omeret ditamah hakkabed umatzea bo taam mar – neemenet, ukeshera.

clarification.explanation: Women are believed regarding tasting the liver. Therefore, if the household did not find the gallbladder, and a woman testifies that she tasted the liver and found a bitter taste in it — she is believed, and the fowl is kosher.
takeaways: A woman's testimony that she tasted a bitter taste in the liver is believed and suffices to permit a fowl missing its gallbladder.

paragraphs: Im chasera hammara, ubadequ bekol hammeqomot velo matzeu taam mar vehitripu hattarnegolet, az la mibbaaya deneesor habbetzim shennimtzeu betokah, ella gam habbetzim shennoledu mimmenna qodem shechita asurot. veim nitarebu habbetzim shennoledu mimmenna qodem shechita im betzim kesherim, yesh lehakshir hattaarobet; v"g deyesh choleqim veoserim hattaarobet - yesh lismok al hammeqillim, vehammachmir, tabo alayv beraka. vekol zeh hu im lo matzeu apillu kis reqan shel hammara vegam lo roshem shello; abal im haya kis reqam o denikkar roshem shello, veraq shello taamu taam mar bakkabed ulekak hitripuha, en leesor ella betzim hannimtzaim betokah, abal betzim sheyyaleda qodem shechita yesh lehattir; veayyen machaziq beraka v"torat-zebach".

clarification.explanation: If the gallbladder is missing and all the locations were checked without finding a bitter taste, and the chicken is thereby disqualified (treifah) — then not only are the eggs found inside it forbidden, but also the eggs the chicken had already laid before slaughter are forbidden (since the animal was already treifah at the time they were laid). If these eggs became mixed with kosher eggs, the mixture may be permitted (although some disagree and forbid it, it is proper to rely on the lenient authorities, and one who is stringent is blessed). All this applies when not even an empty bile sac or a sign of one was found. But if an empty sac or a clear sign that the bile had been there was found (only that no bitter taste was tasted in the liver, and it was therefore disqualified) — then only the eggs found inside the body are forbidden, but the eggs laid before slaughter are permitted.
takeaways: If a chicken is disqualified for a missing gallbladder with no sign of it at all, even eggs laid before slaughter are forbidden; if there was a sign or empty sac, only the internal eggs are forbidden.

paragraphs: Matzeu shette merut – terepa, apillu meruchaqot zo mizzo. veim matzeu mara achat niret kishtayim, yabiu otah lemoreh veyibdoq veyireh: im shopekot zo lezo, achat hi ukeshera; veim lav terepa.

clarification.explanation: If two gallbladders are found in a fowl — it is treifah, even if they are far apart. If one gallbladder is found that appears to be two (as if split), it should be brought to a halachic authority for examination: if they drain into each other (actually connected) — it is a single gallbladder and the fowl is kosher; if not — it is treifah.
takeaways: Two separate gallbladders — treifah; a gallbladder that appears double but is actually connected — kosher, per expert examination.

paragraphs: Hatztzebi en lo mara bakkabed, abal yesh lo mara lematta samuk liznabo. veim lo nimtza bo mara kelal, o im niqqeba hammara shello, o sheyyesh lo shette merut, terepa; veim lo nimtzet samuk lazzanab venimtzet bakkabed, keshera; abal im lo nimtzet bo mara kelal, vetamo hakkabed umetzao mar, la mehanne uterepa. velo od - ella apillu im tamo bazzanab o samuk lazzanab vetamo mar, la mehanne; vaapillu deyesh omerim mehanne, rauy lehachmir, deen beyadenu lehakria bazeh. veyesh mine opot sheen lahem mara kelal, veen leaseran, dekak hu beriyyatan.

clarification.explanation: A deer has no gallbladder in the liver, but rather bile located lower, near its tail. If no bile is found in it at all, or its bile is perforated, or it has two bile sacs — it is treifah. If the bile is not found in its usual location (near the tail) but is found in the liver — it is kosher. But if no bile is found in it at all, and the liver was tasted and found bitter, this does not help, and the deer is treifah — and even if a bitter taste is tasted at or near the tail, this too does not help (some disagree and hold it does help, but it is proper to be stringent, since we cannot decide the matter). There are species of birds that naturally have no gallbladder at all, and these should not be forbidden, since that is how they were created.
takeaways: The deer's law is different: its bile is near the tail, not the liver; a missing bile in it cannot be resolved by tasting bitterness (unlike a fowl).
Species naturally lacking a gallbladder entirely carry no disqualification at all.

paragraphs: Hattechol, "g deshel behema im niqqab, terepa - mikkol maqom techol shel op im niqqab, kasher. veken im kol hattechol shel haop laquy, kasher. vehu haddin im nimtzeu shene techolim beop, kasher; ak hachayya, dinah kibhema; veayyen keneset haggedola, haggahat bet yosep, ot y"d.

clarification.explanation: In a domestic animal, if the spleen is perforated — it is treifah. But in a fowl, a perforated spleen does not disqualify it, and the fowl is kosher. The same applies if the spleen is entirely damaged ("lakui") — it is kosher. And likewise if two spleens are found in a fowl — it is kosher. But in a wild animal (such as a deer), the law is like that of a domestic animal — that is, a perforated spleen disqualifies it.
takeaways: A perforated or damaged spleen in a fowl does not disqualify it (unlike a domestic or wild animal, where a perforated spleen does disqualify it).

paragraphs: Haop en lo kis-hashsheten. veim nimtzet tarnegolet bitnah tzaba, uqerauha achar shechita veyatzeu mimmenna mayim zakkim, yesh libdoq bemeayim verea ubekol ebarim shehanneqeb posel bahem, veim lo nimtza reuta, yesh lehattir behepsed merubbeh; umikkol maqom yesh chashash choli leekol mimmenna vekannizkar baacharonim; laken, shomer napsho yirchaq mizzeh.

clarification.explanation: A fowl has no bladder. If a chicken is found with a swollen belly, and when opened after slaughter clear water emerges from it — one must examine the intestines, the lungs, and every organ whose perforation disqualifies; if no defect is found in them, the chicken may be eaten only in a case of great monetary loss (where there is no other option). Nevertheless, there is a health concern in eating it, as the later authorities wrote, and therefore one who cares for his health should keep away from it.
takeaways: A chicken with a swollen belly and clear water inside is permitted only in case of great loss and after a full examination, and even then carries a health concern best avoided.

paragraphs: Im yatzeu meeha, dehaynu haddaqqin sheqqorin bearbit "mitztzarin", derek neqeb bet-harei, ushechatah beodan bachutz, terepa; velo od, ella apillu im yatzeu vehuchzeru mealehen, gam ken terepa, ki kevan dehammaqom tzar, chayeshinan shemma nithappeku mesadderan. vetzarik lehazhir haam bazeh ki hu dabar hammatzuy betarnegolim, vehashshochet lo yargish bazeh qodem shechita. veod, deim yatzeu vechazeru mealehen, ditrepa - ek yada bazeh hashshochet? veraq bene-habbayit yodeim im naasa bah kak im lav. veim yedeu denaasa bah kak ditrepa, lo yimkeru otah legoy, shemma yimkerenna leyisrael - ella im ken yodea beberur shehaggoy yishchatenna leatzmo; mihu, kol zeh eno ella im yatzeu haddaqqin, abal im yatzea haem shehi hakkarkashta, shemmattelet mishsham habbetzim, keshera; vegam muttar lehachazirah beyadayim, ki yetziatah enah mazzeqet kelal; veayyen "qometz veissaron", seip qatan ' ub'.

clarification.explanation: If the small intestines ("metzarin") protruded through the exit opening (the rectum) and the fowl was slaughtered while they were still outside — it is treifah. And even if the intestines protruded and returned inside on their own — it is likewise treifah, since there is concern they may have twisted from their place due to the narrowness of the passage. The public should be warned about this, since it is a common occurrence in chickens, and the slaughterer himself cannot notice it before slaughter. Household members, who see the chicken after opening it, are the only ones who know if such a thing occurred. If they knew this happened (and the chicken is treifah), it is forbidden to sell it to a gentile without qualification, lest the gentile resell it to another Jew, but only if it is clear the gentile will slaughter it for his own use. But if only the "karkeshta" (the egg-laying part) protruded — the chicken is kosher, and it is even permitted to push it back manually, since its protrusion causes no harm at all.
takeaways: Protrusion of the small intestines through the anus (even if it returned on its own) disqualifies the fowl as treifah; protrusion of the egg-laying part does not disqualify it at all.
One must be careful not to sell such a fowl to a gentile without confirming it is for his own use, out of concern he might resell it to another Jew.

paragraphs: Hattarnegolim hamsorasim - im derek bene hair lesares, amerinan missetama hammitasseq bazeh hu baqi bimlaka zo veeno nogea bibne-meayim, ukesherim hen vekannizkar baacharonim; veken nohagim poh irenu bagdad y", deokelim tarnegolim hamsorasim habbaim min haarbiyyim; dibqiim beserus veen osin nezeq.

clarification.explanation: Castrated roosters (having undergone castration) — if it is the accepted local practice that there are professionals engaged in castration, one assumes that whoever performed it is skilled in his craft and did not touch the intestines in a way causing harm, and therefore they are kosher. This was the practice in Baghdad, eating castrated roosters brought by Arabs, since they were skilled in the craft and caused no harm.
takeaways: Roosters castrated by a skilled professional, where this is the local practice, are kosher, since one assumes he did not harm the intestines.

paragraphs: Lipamim yimtza bebeten hattarnegolim kis qatan male mursa o dam qarush; veken lipamim yimmatze taluy bedaqqin kemo dad qatan - kaasher yizdammenu shinnuyim ellu etzel baalat-habbayit, tebiem lipne hammoreh veyireh; ki lipamim yimmatze betok hakkis o haddad shibre mechittim vekayyotze.

clarification.explanation: Sometimes a small sac full of pus ("morsa") or clotted blood is found in a chicken's belly, and sometimes something resembling a small teat is found hanging in the intestines. In such cases, the woman of the house should bring the finding to a halachic authority for examination, since sometimes needle fragments or other objects are found inside this sac or teat that affect the halachic ruling.
takeaways: Any unusual finding, such as a pus sac or a "teat" in the intestines, should be brought for examination by a halachic authority, since objects (such as needle fragments) may be hidden inside, affecting kashrut.

paragraphs: Haqqurqeban sheqqorin bearbe "gantzi", yimmatze betokah lipamim mechatim qetannim sheqqorin "ebre" (sikkot), velipamim noqebet haqqurqeban meeber leeber, velipamim en nuqbin ella raq besar haqqurqeban; lekak tzarik lahabio lipne hammoreh. gam yimmatze bekares habbehema mechatim techubin bekares o beqeba sheqqorin bearbe "shegaddana" (qeba elyona); vegam zeh yabiu lipne hammoreh veyodia lahem haddin. veim hishliku peresh hakkares veshittepuhu bammayim, ukeshebbau lenaqqoto besakkin mishshiyyure hepresh, rau ober bigriratam machat im hepresh - yesh leesor bazeh "p shello metzauhu tachub bekares, mishshum deim lo haya bachalal hakkares im hepresh, haya yotze veober battechilla im hepresh; veayyen "erek-hashshulchan" v"torat-zebach".

clarification.explanation: In a fowl's gizzard ("gantzi") small needles (pins) are sometimes found, and sometimes the gizzard is perforated all the way through, and sometimes only its outer flesh is perforated — all of these require examination by a halachic authority. Likewise in an animal's rumen or upper stomach ("shegdana") needles are sometimes lodged, and this too should be brought to the authority. A special case: if the rumen's contents were discarded and rinsed with water, and while cleaning residual waste with a knife a needle was seen "passing" together with the waste in the scraping — one should forbid it, since if the needle had not previously been inside the rumen's cavity together with the waste, it would not have emerged together with it in the first place.
takeaways: Finding a needle or a perforation in the gizzard, rumen, or stomach requires examination by a halachic authority; even if the needle was found only while cleaning waste (not directly lodged in the rumen), one should be concerned and forbid it.

paragraphs: Gid hannasheh eno asur ella baakila, abal bahanaa muttar; velaken muttar lehaakilo leopot o litteno legoy; mihu, katab harab "aspaqlarya hammeira" bebeur hazzohar, parashat vayyishlach beshem "zohar chadash" vezeh leshono: minhag yapeh hu beyisrael keshemmesirin gid hannasheh - shezzoreqin umedabbeqin oto beqorot o beqirot habbayit, leharot lesitra achara shehu shalem veqayyam; vezeh gorem shemmitchazzeqim haashirim laasot sammekin leorayeta. venireh li dehaynu tama name shemminhag beyisrael lehadbiq beqorot ubeqirot habbayit enunita devarda shemmunnach bakkis; ad kan leshono bedap k"d. velo beer harab tamo dimdamme enunita devarda legid hannasheh. veayyen zohar pinechas, dap rl" vedap rl"d, besod hayyoteret sheal hakkabed, ayyen sham. vehinneh mvr"m za"l besiman s"h hebi hamminhag lehashlik enunita devarda velo leakelah; veayyen keneset haggedola, siman l"h, haggahat hattur, ot z', shehebin hattaam mishshum meus; ubeemet milleshon mvr"m za"l nireh detaam hammeus qae al basar laban vedaq davqa. vehinneh poh irenu bagdad nohagim leekol enunita devarda, ak zehu maakal aniyyim poh irenu. veek sheyyihyeh - begid hannasheh rauy lehazhiram kemo shekkatab harab za"l, abal beenunita devarda en lehazhiram kelum. veda ki poh irenu nohagin lehashlik kol havveshatin veen okelin havveshet; venireh deen bazeh mishshum geder issur kelal, ella raq hu mishshum digrii ninehu veen bahem taam basar, lekak mashlikim otam; veayin shabbat, dap qk"b unedarim dap n"b, yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: The sciatic nerve is forbidden only for eating, but is permitted for benefit — therefore it is permitted to feed it to fowl or give it to a gentile. Rabbi Yosef Chaim brings a lovely custom from the Zohar: when the sciatic nerve is removed, it is thrown and stuck onto the beams or walls of the house, to show the "Sitra Achra" (the force of evil) that it remains whole and intact — and this strengthens wealthy people to support Torah study. Rabbi Yosef Chaim speculates that for the same reason it was customary to also stick up the "einunita d'varda" (a gland found in the scrotal sac), though he did not explicitly explain why he compared it to the sciatic nerve. Regarding the mystical secret involved, he refers to the Zohar, Parashat Pinchas, which discusses "the secret of the lobe upon the liver" (a part of the liver carrying a hidden kabbalistic significance) — meaning, beyond the simple law of permissibility and benefit, there is also an additional kabbalistic layer to these matters. The Rema cited the custom of discarding the einunita d'varda and not eating it, and commentators explained this is due to repulsiveness. But in Baghdad it was customary to eat it, as food for the poor. The conclusion: regarding the sciatic nerve, the public should be warned (following the Zohar's custom), but regarding the einunita d'varda there is no need to warn. It was likewise customary in Baghdad to discard the esophagus and not eat it, not due to any prohibition but because it is poor and lacks the taste of meat.
takeaways: The sciatic nerve is permitted for benefit (feeding animals or giving to a gentile), forbidden only for eating; there is a custom to stick it to a wall as a symbol.
The einunita d'varda (a certain gland) and the esophagus are not halachically forbidden, though some places avoid them out of repulsiveness or lack of taste.

Rabbi Yosef Chaim refers to the Zohar, Parashat Pinchas, on "the secret of the lobe upon the liver" — hinting that these liver-adjacent parts also carry a hidden kabbalistic significance beyond the simple laws of permissibility and benefit.

paragraphs: Kol op ubehema, im yishchatu acheret lepaneha, titztammeq rea shellah mechamat happachad; veqayma lan: rea shetztzameqa kullah vaapillu rubbah, im mechamat bene-adam shehipchiduha kegon sheshshachatu acheret lepaneha vekayyotze bazeh, hare zeh terepa. veal-ken beir gedola shebbaim bene-adam harbeh bebat-achat ubeyadam tarnegolim, vehashshochet shochet lipnehem tarnegolim - la arik lemebad haki laamod etzel hashshochet sheshshochet, vehem ochazim tarnegolim chayyim beyadam, deyesh bazeh chashash tzimmuq harea vegam tzaar baale chayyim, ella tzarik sheyyitrachaqu meat meetzel hashshochet, beopen shello yiru hattarnegolim shebbeyadam hashshechita.

clarification.explanation: A halachic rule: any fowl or animal that witnesses another animal being slaughtered in front of it may have its lungs shrink from fear. And it was ruled: a lung that shrank entirely or mostly due to a fright caused by people (for example, another animal being slaughtered in front of it) — is treifah. Therefore, in a large city where many people arrive simultaneously with live chickens to the slaughterer, it is not proper to stand near the slaughterer holding live chickens in hand while he is slaughtering others — since there is concern this may shrink the lungs of the waiting chickens, and it also causes suffering to the animals. One should step back somewhat from the slaughterer so the waiting chickens do not witness the slaughter.
takeaways: Animals awaiting slaughter should be kept away from the slaughtering site itself, to prevent lung shrinkage from fright (which would disqualify them) and to prevent animal suffering.

paragraphs: Kol eprocha op shennolad, asur leshachatu uleakelo ki im ad sheyyigdelu hakkenapayim, dehaynu notza sheal gupo sheyyesh lah qanim, vekannizkar bapposeqim, beyoreh dea, siman t"v. veim lo gadelu hannotzot veshachatu - "g deharab peri toar za"l, seip qatan ' mattir bediabad - yesh oserin, venakon lehachmir kisbaratam.

clarification.explanation: A newly hatched chick may not be slaughtered and eaten until its wings have grown — that is, the feathers on its body have developed quills (matured). If it was slaughtered before the feathers grew — there is a lenient opinion (Pri To'ar) permitting it after the fact, but some forbid it, and it is proper to be stringent following their view.
takeaways: A chick should not be slaughtered before its feathers have developed; it is proper to be stringent even after the fact if it was slaughtered too early.

paragraphs: Valad shel behema, "g demaran za"l mattir leshachatu miyyad beet shennolad im yadua shekkalu lo tisha chodashim, mikkol maqom katebu haacharonim: haiddana la beqiinan bekullo chodashayv, ubekullan tzarik lehamtin shiba yamim meet shennolad; veim abar ushechato qodem z' yamim, asur leakelo; mihu, la baenan z' yamim meet leet - sheim nolad besop hayyom, chashebinan leyom halleda leyom gamur, veachar shishsha yamim meoto hayyom shochato vekannizkar baacharonim za"l. vehayyisrael sheomer: zeh ben ch' yamim, neeman; abal haggoy eno neeman apillu mesicha lepi tummo; veen lismok bazzeman hazzeh al simanim shekkatebu happoseqim bedabar zeh, leda im hu ben ch', ki teba hazzeman nishtanna vekannizkar baacharonim.

clarification.explanation: A newborn animal — although Maran (the Shulchan Aruch) permits slaughtering it immediately upon birth if it is clearly known to have completed nine months of gestation — the later authorities wrote that in our time we are not expert enough to know with certainty whether it completed its months, and therefore in every case one must wait seven days from its birth before slaughtering. If it was slaughtered before seven days passed — it is forbidden to eat. An exact "day for day" count of seven days is not required: if it was born at the end of the day, that day is considered a full day, and after six more days it may be slaughtered. The testimony of a Jew stating "this is an eight-day-old newborn" is believed, but a gentile's testimony is not believed even if stated incidentally. One should not rely in our time on the external signs the authorities wrote for identifying the newborn's age, since the nature of the times has changed.
takeaways: In our time one must wait seven days from an animal's birth before slaughter, and not rely on knowledge that it completed nine months of gestation or on external signs.
A Jew's testimony about the newborn's age is believed; a gentile's is not.

paragraphs: Oto veet beno asur lishchot beyom echad - ben adam echad, ben shene bene-adam - la shena haem veaach"k habben o habbat, la shena lehepek. vekol shehu karuk achareha, chazaqa shehi immo, vekol shekken yoneq mimmenna; vaapillu im haem z vehabbat rachel o ippeka, im karuk achareha asur leshachatam beyom echad, veayyen "simla chadasha"; veim lo karuk achareha velo yoneq mimmenna, "p sheddomeh letoar haem o bishar simanin shebbaggup, en chosheshin min hassapeq umuttar lishchot vekannizkar bapposeqim. v"g dehaddabar sapeq etzlenu im din oto veet beno noheg bazzekarim o eno noheg, haynu davqa leinyan malqut, abal issura ikka; laken im noda lanu beberur shezzeh abiv, kegon shehaya hazzakar shehu haab, im hanneqeba bebayit echad lebaddam, ubarur lanu shennitabbera mimmennu, az asur lishchot haab vehabben beyom echad; abal im lo nitbarer haddabar beopen zeh shehu abiv, en chosheshin umuttar leshachatu, apillu roin havvalad karuk achare hazzakar.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to slaughter a mother and her offspring (son or daughter) on the same day — whether the same person slaughters both, or two different people, and regardless of the order (mother first or offspring first). Any offspring that follows closely after a certain animal (and certainly if it nurses from her) — there is a presumption that she is its mother, even if, for example, the mother is a goat and the offspring appears to be a lamb or vice versa. If the offspring does not follow after the animal and does not nurse from her, there is no concern for doubt, even if it resembles her in appearance or other traits, and slaughter is permitted. The doubt whether the law of "it and its offspring" also applies to males (father and son) concerns only the penalty of lashes, but the prohibition itself exists; therefore if it is clearly known that this is the father (for example, the father and mother were alone together and it is clear the offspring is from him), it is forbidden to slaughter the father and son on the same day. But if this is not clearly known, there is no concern and slaughter is permitted, even if the offspring follows after that same male.
takeaways: It is forbidden to slaughter a mother and her offspring on the same day when there is a presumption of motherhood (following her/nursing from her) — regardless of order or who slaughters.
The law applies also to a father and his son when it is clearly known he is the father, even though the penalty for this is disputed.

paragraphs: Abar veshachat beyom echad, "g demaran za"l satam lehattir leakelam bo bayyom - yesh oserin leekol haacharon bo bayyom, ella yamtin ad hallayla mishshum qenas; abal harishon la abid beh issura, veyakol leakelo bo bayyom; vekatebu haacharonim lehachmir kedibre haoserim vaapillu sheshshachat beshogeg; mihu, gam ledibre haoserim, en asur ella lashshochet atzmo, veken labbealim sheshshachat bishbilam, abal laacherim muttar; veyesh machmirim leesor gam laacherim. veayyen "tebuot-shor" v"erek-hashshulchan". veyom echad haamur beoto veet beno, hayyom holek achar hallayla. ketzad? shachat harishon bitchillat lel rebii - lo yishchot hashsheni ad techillat lel chamishi; veim shachat harishon besop yom rebii qodem ben hashshemashot - shochet hashsheni bitchillat lel chamishi; veim shachat achar ben-hashshemashot shel lel chamishi - lo yishchot hashsheni ad lel shishshi vadday, abal lo yishchat beben-hashshemashot delel shishshi, deshemma ben hashshemashot harishon haya layla uben hashshemashot hashsheni hu yom.

clarification.explanation: One who transgressed and slaughtered a mother and her offspring on the same day — although Maran (the Shulchan Aruch) permits eating both without qualification on that day, some forbid eating the second one slaughtered that day (as a penalty), requiring one to wait until night; but the first one (in which there was no prohibition) may be eaten immediately. The later authorities wrote to be stringent following the stricter view, even if the second slaughter was done unintentionally. But even according to the stricter view, the prohibition applies only to the slaughterer himself and the owner for whom it was slaughtered, but is permitted to others (some are stringent to forbid it to others as well). Regarding the definition of "one day" for this prohibition — the day follows the night that preceded it. For example: if he slaughtered the first at the start of Wednesday night, it is forbidden to slaughter the second until the start of Thursday night; and if he slaughtered the first at the end of Wednesday (before twilight), it is permitted to slaughter the second already at the start of Thursday night; and if he slaughtered during the twilight of Thursday night (an uncertain time), it is forbidden to slaughter the second until Friday night is certain (but also not during the twilight of Friday night, out of concern the first twilight was still night while the second was already day).
takeaways: Slaughtering a mother and offspring on the same day by mistake — one should be stringent and wait until night to eat the second, even though the primary prohibition applies only to the slaughterer/owner.
The definition of "one day" depends on the twilight boundaries and requires special care during the border hours between days.

paragraphs: Yesh dabar echad shennikshalin bo rabbim, umatzuy hu bimdinot ellu: sheyyesh yisreelim sheyyesh lahem tzon leravach haggizza vehechalab vehavveladot, shemmoserim otam leroeh, veen leroeh shuttaput begup hatztzon kelal, raq loqeach cheleq min hechalab vehatztzemer; veellu hatztzon molidim kol shana, veyesh bah harbeh tzon shemmolidim bekorot shehem qodesh, vetzarik lehazhiram laasot tiqqun lazeh, sheyyaasu shuttaput kepi haddin legoy begup habbehemot, vaapillu cheleq echad mimmea saggi leh bazeh, vaalehem tabo birkat tob.

clarification.explanation: A common pitfall: Jews who keep flocks for the benefit of wool shearing, milk, and offspring hand them over to a shepherd who has no partnership whatsoever in the animals' bodies themselves (he only receives a share of the milk and wool). These flocks give birth every year, and many of the offspring are firstborns, whose law is sanctified (carrying the sanctity of a firstborn animal). Flock owners should be warned to correct this in advance: to form a genuine partnership (even one part in a hundred suffices) with a gentile in the bodies of the animals themselves, in order to prevent the offspring from carrying the sanctity of a firstborn — and one who does so is blessed.
takeaways: Flock owners should form a partnership (even a minimal one) with a gentile in the animals' bodies, to prevent firstborn offspring from carrying the sanctity of a firstborn, which requires special halachic handling.
